title: Welcome: Course Map and Table of Contents
summary: See the whole course at a glance: what you will learn each week, how each unit is built, how you will be assessed and how to get the most from the training.

p: This course teaches you how to keep children and adults safe from harm caused by an organisation's own people and activities. It also teaches you how to train others to do the same. That is why it is called a Training of Trainers (ToT) and capacity building course.

It is written in simple words. You do not need to know the law or to have worked in safeguarding before. If you are a teacher, a school leader, a programme officer, a volunteer coordinator or a community worker, this course is for you.
What you will be able to do at the end:
• Explain what safeguarding is and what it is not.
• Spot abuse, power imbalances and safeguarding risks in real situations.
• Explain the main laws that protect children in Nigeria and Lagos.
• Check a safeguarding policy and turn it into working procedures.
• Build a safeguarding culture in your school or organisation.
• Carry out a safeguarding risk assessment, score the risks and escalate them.
• Recruit and induct staff and volunteers safely.
• Set up reporting channels that people will use, and respond well to a disclosure.
• Plan, teach and follow up a safeguarding awareness session for others.

img.cap: Every child has the right to be safe. Photo from the training materials.

b: Teachers, school heads and school safeguarding leads.
Programme staff, field officers and community volunteers.
Managers, HR officers, finance and procurement staff.
Anyone who will train colleagues, partners or communities.

• Unit 1: Welcome, course map and table of contents.
• Unit 2: What safeguarding is, key terms, what it is not, and the four pillars.
• Unit 3: Power, vulnerability and consent.

• Unit 5: International standards and the six core principles.

• Unit 9: What safeguarding needs, and safeguarding assessments.
• Unit 10: The must-have policies and what every policy must contain.
• Unit 11: From policy to procedure, tools, templates, consultation and putting it into practice.
Week 4: Culture and roles
• Unit 12: Building and sustaining a safeguarding culture.
• Unit 13: Roles and responsibilities, writing safeguarding into job descriptions, and the SFP/DSL role.
Week 5: Safe programming, risk assessment and safer recruitment
• Unit 14: Safe programming, risk triggers and risk categories.
• Unit 15: Types of risk assessment, the procedure, scoring and escalation.
• Unit 16: Safer spaces, safe partnerships and risk assessment in practice.

b: 22 units over 6 weeks.
Short practice questions at the end of each unit (they do not count towards your final score).
A 100-question end-of-course assessment. You need 75% to pass.
Activities and templates to use in your own organisation.

p: Every unit follows the same pattern, so you always know what to expect.
• Short explanation in simple words, with key terms defined.
• Bullet points for the main ideas.
• Examples and scenarios from real settings in Nigeria and Lagos.
• Worked tools: tables, checklists and templates you can copy.
• A 'Try it yourself' activity for your own organisation.
• Three practice questions to check your understanding.
How to study:
• Read one section at a time. Stop and think about your own organisation.
• Do the activity before you move on. Writing things down helps you remember.
• If you can, study with a colleague and compare your answers.
• Keep a notebook for your action plan. You will use it in the last unit.

img.alt: An open notebook and pen on a wooden table
img.cap: Keep a notebook for your notes and your action plan.

b: Two or three study sessions of 60 to 90 minutes.
One session to do the activities with a colleague.
A short review on the last day: answer the practice questions again.

sections.h: What the final assessment is like
p: At the end of the course you take one assessment with 100 multiple-choice questions.
Key facts:
• The questions are difficult. They test whether you can apply what you learned, not only remember it.
• Each question has four options. The options are written to look alike, so you must think carefully.
• You need 75% to pass and earn your course certificate.
• Only the final assessment counts. The practice questions in each unit do not add to your score.
Tips:
• Read each question twice and look at every option.
• Look for words such as 'first', 'best', 'most likely' and 'not'.
• Think about the survivor's safety first. It is usually the key to the best answer.

b: Write down one safeguarding situation from your own work that you want to understand better.
Write down one thing you hope to change in your organisation.
Read your notes again at the end of the course.

title: What Safeguarding Is, Key Terms and the Four Pillars
summary: Define safeguarding and related terms, learn what safeguarding is not, and understand the four pillars: awareness, prevention, reporting and response.

p: Safeguarding is the responsibility of every organisation to make sure its staff, operations and programmes do no harm to children, adults and staff. This includes contractors, partners and representatives. It also means protecting them from abuse, exploitation and neglect.
The safeguarding question: could our people, or our activities, cause harm here?
• Child safeguarding covers everyone under 18.
• Adult safeguarding covers adults at risk, staff and community members that our work reaches.
• Safeguarding is about harm caused by us or our work. It is not only about harm that happens in families or the community.

img.alt: Silhouette of a child at a window with hands on the glass
img.cap: Safeguarding means keeping every child safe, including from harm that could come from our own people.

b: A volunteer who runs a weekend class offers one girl 'extra lessons' alone at his house. This is a safeguarding concern about our own volunteer.
A child who is beaten at home is a child protection concern, and the organisation may help, but the harm was not caused by our people.

sections.h: Key related terms: define and explain
p: Learn these terms. Each one is used in the rest of the course.
• PSEAH: Protection from Sexual Exploitation, Abuse and Harassment. The commitments, systems and actions that stop staff and representatives from sexually exploiting, abusing or harassing anyone.
• Sexual exploitation: any real or attempted abuse of a position of vulnerability, unequal power or trust for sexual purposes, including gaining money, social or political benefit.
• Sexual abuse: actual or threatened physical intrusion of a sexual nature, by force or under unequal or forced conditions.
• Sexual harassment: unwelcome sexual behaviour that creates an intimidating, hostile or offensive environment, often between colleagues.
• Duty of care: the legal and moral duty to take reasonable steps to keep the people we work with safe from harm we can foresee.
• Do No Harm: our presence, programmes and people must never make anyone less safe than before we arrived.
• Accountability: being answerable to the people we serve, not only to donors. Communities know what to expect, can give feedback and complain, and see us act on it.

• Social safeguards: standards used by funders and development banks so that projects do not harm people or communities (labour conditions, community health and safety, and protection of vulnerable groups).
• Risk: the chance that harm happens, combined with how serious the harm would be. Safeguarding risk is about harm to people, not money or reputation.

b: Exploitation uses someone's weaker position for your own gain.
Abuse is harm done to a person, often by someone who has power over them.
Harassment is unwelcome behaviour that makes someone feel unsafe or uncomfortable at work.

p: Safeguarding overlaps with other ideas, but it is different. Being clear stops confusion.
• Safety: general physical safety such as fire exits, hard hats and preventing accidents. Safeguarding protects people from deliberate harm, abuse, exploitation and neglect by others.
• Child protection: reacts to known or suspected harm to a specific child. Safeguarding is broader and acts before harm happens, for all children and adults at risk.

• Security: protects the organisation and staff from outside threats such as theft or data breaches. Safeguarding protects beneficiaries and communities from harm caused by people inside or linked to the organisation.
• Risk management: looks at organisation risks such as money, reputation and operations. Safeguarding focuses on the risk of harm to vulnerable people.
• HR or conduct matters: staff complaints, discipline and employment issues. A safeguarding concern may start an HR process, but it is not the same thing.

• Safeguarding vs protection: safeguarding keeps people safe from harm caused by us and our work. Protection (for example child protection) responds to harm children face in their families and communities.

b: A broken fire exit is a safety issue.
A stolen laptop is a security issue.
A teacher who is hitting a pupil is a safeguarding issue.
A late payment to a vendor is a financial risk, not a safeguarding risk.

p: A strong safeguarding system rests on four pillars. If one is weak, the system is weak.
Pillar 1: Awareness. People know what safeguarding is, what harm looks like and what to do.
• Know your safeguarding policy, the signs of abuse and who the vulnerable people are in your work.
• Know your role. Communities should know their rights and how to report.
• Methods: training, induction and briefings.
Pillar 2: Prevention. Stop harm before it happens through policies, training, good practice, safe environments and safe programmes.
• Risk assessments before activities, safe programme design and a strong safeguarding culture.
• Code of conduct enforcement, safe recruitment and clear power and accountability structures.
Pillar 3: Reporting. Safe, easy ways for anyone, inside or outside the organisation, to raise a concern.
• Clear channels, several options, confidentiality, protection from retaliation and quick acknowledgement.
Pillar 4: Response. Act quickly and correctly when harm happens or is suspected.
• Survivor-centred approach, follow the policy, do not investigate alone, escalate and learn from the case.

ex.t: Self-check: where is your organisation strongest?
b: Awareness: do all staff and children know how to report?
Prevention: are risk assessments done before activities?
Reporting: can someone report without fear?
Response: does someone act within 24 hours?

title: Power, Vulnerability and Consent
summary: Understand how power creates risk, why consent is only real when a person is free to say no, and practise spotting who holds the power in real situations.

sections.h: Safeguarding is about the misuse of power
p: In every organisation some people have more power than others. People with less power are at greater risk of exploitation and abuse.
Key points:

• SEAH (sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment) happens when people inside organisations use their power harmfully against people with less power. This can be in their team, in partner organisations or in the communities they serve.
• SEAH affects women and girls most, but it also affects men and boys.
• Consent is real only when a person is free to say no. If one person controls food, pay, a job, a place to sleep or someone's safety, 'agreement' may not be free consent at all.
• Power is not fixed. Context changes who holds it.

img.alt: Two women talking at a table
img.cap: Whenever one person has more power than the other, take extra care.

b: A field officer registers families for support. He says to a mother, 'If you spend time with me, your name will be on the list.' Her 'yes' is not free consent.
A supervisor asks a junior staff member for a favour and holds the power to renew her contract. Her 'yes' may be fear.

p: Power comes from many places. Learn to name them.
• Gender, age, role and seniority.
• Employment status (permanent or temporary).
• Control of money, food or other resources.
• Education level and knowledge.
• Disability.
• Nationality or ethnicity.
• Who holds information, and who is believed.
Questions to ask when you look at any relationship:
• Who can give or take something the other person needs?
• Who would be believed if something went wrong?
• Who can leave, and who cannot?
• Who is alone, and who has witnesses?

b: The same person can have power in one setting and little power in another.
A teacher has power over pupils in school, but less power than a head teacher.
A child worker may depend on an employer for food and a bed.

p: Work in pairs. For each pair of people below, decide who has more power and why. Think about age, money, information, control of movement and who would be believed.
Scenarios:
• A: A caseworker and a 14-year-old girl who receives support. Think about access, trust and control of support.
• B: A field officer who registers families and a mother hoping to be enrolled. Think about gatekeeping, need and gender.
• C: A volunteer who runs a weekend class and the children who attend. Think about trust, authority and private contact.
• D: A driver and a child travelling to an activity. Think about being alone, no witnesses and age.
• E: A staff member taking photos for a donor report and the children in the activity. Think about consent and who decides what is shared.
• F: The Executive Director and the safeguarding focal person who must report a concern about a senior colleague. Think about seniority, job security and fear.
• G: A senior manager and a junior staff member or intern. Think about contracts, references and credibility.
• H: A child domestic worker and the employer she lives and works with. Think about dependence, control and credibility.
Then ask: does the power shift in a different setting? What could the less powerful person do if something went wrong?

ex.t: Model thinking for scenario D (driver and child)
b: Power: the driver is an adult, controls the car and the route, and may be alone with the child.
Risk: no witnesses, the child may not be believed, the child cannot leave.
Safeguards: vetted drivers, headcounts, no child alone with a driver, consent for travel.

sections.h: Activity: map where power sits in your programme
p: A power map is a simple drawing of the people in a programme and who has power over whom. It shows where harm could happen and where your safeguards must be strongest.
How to make one:
• Pick one programme, ideally one that reaches child domestic workers or other children at risk.
• Write everyone involved: children, caregivers, staff, volunteers, drivers, partners, vendors, community leaders, employers.
• Draw arrows from the person with more power to the person with less. Note where the power comes from (money, access, information, status).
• Circle the risky moments: where a less powerful person is alone, dependent or cannot say no.
• For each circle, write one safeguard you already have, or one you need.
You will use this map again when you do a risk assessment in Week 5.

img.alt: A trainer writing on a flip chart
img.cap: Draw your power map on a flip chart or in your notebook.

ex.t: Example of a circle on a power map
b: Home visit to a child domestic worker: a staff member alone with the child in the employer's house.
Safeguard: visit in pairs, meet in a visible space, debrief afterwards.

activity: Draw a power map for one programme in your organisation. Circle at least three risky moments and write one safeguard for each. Show your map to a colleague and ask: what did I miss?

title: Why Safeguarding Matters: The Nigerian Context and the Human Reasons
summary: Learn the legal, practical and human reasons for safeguarding and how to explain them to colleagues in your own words.

sections.h: Why safeguarding matters in Nigeria and Africa
p: Safeguarding is not only a donor rule. It protects real people and strengthens organisations.
• Legal duty: the Child Rights Act, Nigerian labour laws and international standards require it.
• Proof of systems: communities and donors want proof that safeguarding systems are strong.
• Prevention of harm: abuse harms people, so we prevent it. It also prevents loss of life and damage to reputation.
• Saves money and helps raise money: prevention costs far less than a crisis, and strong systems attract funding.
• Protects staff: it protects staff from false accusations and organisations from legal liability.
• Builds culture: a culture of accountability, trust and openness.
• Duty of care: anyone who works with vulnerable groups has this duty, with no exceptions.

img.alt: A team sitting around a table listening
img.cap: Safeguarding is everyone's job, from leaders to volunteers.

b: Which reason matters most to you? Write it on a sticky note or in your notebook.
Why did you choose it? Share your answer with a colleague.

p: When you train others, the human reasons are often more powerful than the legal ones. Use them.
• You are someone's safety net: for a vulnerable person you might be the only one who notices. Your attention could save a life.
• Prevention creates future joy: every child who is protected gets to enjoy childhood and every family kept safe stays whole.
• Safeguarding protects staff too: clear processes protect you from false accusations and from awkward or unsafe situations.
• Cycles of harm stop here: people who are not protected carry pain into adult life. Your action can change a family's story.
• Communities thrive on trust: when safeguarding fails, trust is lost. Your commitment strengthens everyone's sense of safety.
• It is about real people: when you know who you are protecting and why, being alert becomes natural.

ex.t: A short story you can tell
b: A volunteer noticed that a girl in the class stopped speaking and began coming late. He did not ask her directly. He told the safeguarding lead the same day.
The lead spoke to the girl gently, with a second adult, and found she was being harassed on the way home. The family was supported and the problem stopped.
Lesson: small signs matter, and reporting early protects the child.

p: Some people think safeguarding is too expensive or takes too much time. Look at the cost of doing nothing.
• A child is hurt, which is the greatest cost.
• Staff and volunteers may be accused and lose their jobs and good names.
• The organisation may face legal action and lose funding.
• Communities may lose trust and stop sending children to your programmes.
• Other organisations suffer too, because trust in the whole sector is damaged.
The cost of doing it well:
• Time for training, a safeguarding lead with protected time, a small budget for materials and reporting channels.
• These costs are much lower than the costs above.

ex.t: Make the case to your leader
b: Write three sentences: the risk, the cost of doing nothing, the cost of acting.
Use one real example from your own context, without naming people.
Ask for one decision: for example, a named safeguarding lead with time and a budget.

sections.h: What you can do in the next 30 days
p: Start small. These actions cost little and build momentum.
• Read your organisation's safeguarding policy and code of conduct.
• Find out who your safeguarding focal person is, and who the backup is.
• Ask three colleagues if they know how to report a concern.
• Put a reporting poster in one visible place.
• Add a five-minute safeguarding item to your next team meeting.
• Write down one risk in your work and one way to reduce it.
Remember: you do not need to be an expert to begin. You need to care and to act.

b: At the start of every team meeting, ask: 'Is there any safeguarding concern or learning to share?'
Write the answer in the meeting notes.

activity: Choose the three reasons for safeguarding that matter most in your setting. Write one sentence for each that you could say to a colleague who thinks safeguarding is 'just a donor rule'.
